prompt: A processor emits each window two minutes after it ends by its own clock. What goes wrong when the topic is replayed the next day?

choices.text: Nothing, as long as the processor's clock is synchronised with NTP
choices.why: A correct clock still measures the replay's moment, which has nothing to do with the events.

choices.text: The windows close at moments unrelated to the events, so results differ
choices.why: Right. That is processing time, with lesson 9's flaw: the answer depends on when it ran.

choices.text: Every window is emitted twice, once for the original run and once for the replay
choices.why: A replay starts fresh; the problem is which events each window contains.

choices.text: The replay is refused by Kafka
choices.why: Kafka is glad to be read again; that is what a log is for.

prompt: What does a processor actually know that lets it estimate how far time has got?

choices.text: The time of the wall clock where it runs
choices.why: That is processing time, which says nothing about the events.

choices.text: How many events each partition will send
choices.why: Nothing tells it that in advance.

choices.text: The event times it has already seen
choices.why: Right. They move forward, unevenly, and they are the raw material of the watermark.

choices.text: A signal each till sends when it has finished a minute
choices.why: No till sends one; Natal's did not even say it was holding sales.

prompt: A processor's assertion "I do not expect any more events older than this time" is called a ___.
The latest event time seen is 09:12:30 and the bound is 2 minutes. How many seconds after 09:10:00 is the watermark?
Bound 3 minutes. Event times arrive in this order: 10:00:00, 10:04:00, 10:02:00, 10:06:30, 10:05:00. How many minutes after 10:00 is the watermark after the last one?
hint: The latest seen is not the last to arrive.

prompt: A sale from 09:08:50 arrives after one from 09:13:05. Why does the watermark not move back?

choices.text: Old sales are discarded before the watermark sees them
choices.why: Whether it is discarded depends on the watermark; the watermark comes first.

choices.text: It would reopen windows already emitted
choices.why: Right. It is the latest time seen, and that is still 09:13:05.

choices.text: The watermark only uses the first event of each window
choices.why: It uses the latest event time seen, whatever its window.

choices.text: Kafka sorts the partition before the processor reads it
choices.why: A partition is in arrival order; nothing sorts it.

prompt: When is a perfect watermark, one that is never wrong, possible?

choices.text: When the bound is larger than the longest delay any event has ever had
choices.why: Any bound can be beaten by a source that holds events longer, as Natal did.

choices.text: When the topic uses LogAppendTime
choices.why: That makes the stamp the broker's, but the event time inside can still be out of order.

choices.text: When the processor runs on the same machine as the broker
choices.why: Where it runs says nothing about the order of the events.

choices.text: When a source writes its events in order, with no buffering
choices.why: Right. Then it knows how far it has got; real systems almost never are like that.

prompt: In `watermark.py` with a 2-minute bound, after which sale number are the windows 09:00 and 09:05 emitted?
With no lateness, sale 8 (09:08:50) is dropped. The watermark when it arrived was 09:11:05. Why is it too late?

choices.text: It happened more than two minutes before the latest sale
choices.why: That alone would not drop it; what matters is whether its window has been passed.

choices.text: Its window ended at 09:10, and the watermark had passed that
choices.why: Right. The window was emitted and, with no lateness, forgotten.

choices.text: Natal's sales go to the late topic, whatever the watermark says
choices.why: Natal's sales 2 and 5 were counted normally.

choices.text: The watermark moved back when it arrived
choices.why: It never moves back.

prompt: With a 2-minute bound and no lateness, how many cents does the program report for the window 09:05 to 09:10?
Why does sale 6 make the program emit two windows at once?

choices.text: It belongs to both windows
choices.why: Tumbling windows do not overlap; sale 6 is in 09:10 to 09:15.

choices.text: The program emits windows in pairs, the earlier of the two first
choices.why: Sale 10 emits one.

choices.text: It moves the watermark six minutes, past two windows' ends
It is the first sale of a new hour, so every open window is closed
choices.why: It is from 09:12; the hour has nothing to do with it.

prompt: With 5 minutes of lateness, sale 8 updates the 09:05 window. Sale 11 (09:04:30) is still dropped. Why?

choices.text: Its window ended at 09:05, so it was forgotten when the watermark passed 09:10
choices.why: Right. When it arrived the watermark was 09:19:00.

choices.text: Lateness applies only to the window being emitted at that moment
choices.why: It applies to every window, counted from each one's end.

choices.text: A window can be updated only once
choices.why: There is no such limit; any number of late sales may update a kept window.

choices.text: Natal's sales are excluded from late updates
choices.why: Sale 8 is also Natal's, and it was counted.

prompt: Late updates go to a reader that appends each result as a new row and sums the column. What happens to the 09:05 window?

choices.text: Nothing, because the second result replaces the first
choices.why: Replacing is what an upsert does; an append keeps both.

choices.text: Sales 4 and 5 are counted twice
choices.why: Right. There are two rows for one window, and the sum adds both.

choices.text: Sale 8 is lost
choices.why: It is in the second row; the trouble is the first row is still there too.

choices.text: The processor refuses to emit an update to an appending reader
choices.why: The processor does not know how its output is read.

prompt: Five-minute tumbling windows and 30 minutes of allowed lateness. How many extra windows per key are kept open at any moment because of the lateness?
Match each engine's setting to what it decides.

pairs.right: when a window is first emitted
how long an emitted window is kept for updates
both: the window accepts records until stream time passes end plus grace
where events too late for any window go

right_distractors: how many partitions a topic has

prompt: What does sending late sales to their own topic give you that dropping them does not?

choices.text: They are counted in the window after all
choices.why: The window is gone; the topic is a record, not a way back in.

choices.text: The processor runs faster
choices.why: Producing a record costs about the same as dropping it.

choices.text: The watermark moves back to include them
choices.why: It never moves back.

choices.text: A trail of them, to count and inspect
choices.why: Right. Late data stops being invisible.

prompt: The number of late events per hour on the late topic jumps a hundredfold one afternoon. What is the most likely reading?

choices.text: The bound is too large and should be shortened
choices.why: A bound too large produces fewer late events, not more.

choices.text: Kafka lost the watermark
choices.why: Kafka does not hold the watermark; the processor computes it.

choices.text: A till, a network or a clock went wrong
choices.why: Right. A bound that fits produces a steady trickle; a jump is a change in the stream.

choices.text: Sales doubled that afternoon
choices.why: Twice the sales would give twice the late events, not a hundred times.

prompt: In the measured day, 292 of 360 sales had a distance of 0, 311 were within 60 seconds and 322 within 120. How many sales does raising the bound from 1 minute to 2 minutes save from being late?
p85 of the distance is 40 seconds and p90 is 1,847 seconds. What does the jump say about choosing the bound?

choices.text: Use the p90, half an hour, since 90% is the usual target
choices.why: That makes every result wait half an hour to catch a few of Natal's held sales.

choices.text: Use the average distance
choices.why: The average mixes the two populations and fits neither.

choices.text: Pick a bound just past the first group; the gap means the second needs other tools
choices.why: Right. Lateness, a late topic and the nightly batch handle the hours-late group.

choices.text: Use no bound at all, since most sales arrive in order
choices.why: With no bound, every slow delivery of seconds becomes late.

prompt: With a 6-minute bound instead of 2, what did the twelve sales gain and lose?

choices.text: Gained nothing, lost latency
choices.why: Sale 8 was counted, which it was not with 2 minutes.

choices.text: Sale 8 counted; the 09:05 window emitted four sales later
choices.why: Right. Completeness bought with latency.

choices.text: Both late sales were counted, and the windows were emitted at the same moments
choices.why: Sale 11 was still dropped, and the windows waited longer.

choices.text: Lost sale 8, gained speed
choices.why: It is the other way round: a larger bound waits longer and loses less.

prompt: Why does a processor take the LOWEST of its partitions' watermarks?

choices.text: A lagging partition still has earlier events to deliver
choices.why: Right. There is no order between partitions, so time has only got as far as the slowest.

choices.text: The lowest is cheaper to compute
choices.why: Any of them is one comparison; the reason is correctness.

choices.text: Kafka requires it
choices.why: Kafka has no watermark; the processor chooses the rule.

choices.text: To emit results as early as possible
choices.why: The lowest is the latest to emit, not the earliest.

prompt: Three partitions have latest event times 09:21:00, 09:12:30 and 09:17:45. With a 2-minute bound, how many minutes after 09:00 is the watermark?
A topic has 12 partitions and Ponto Final's five shops as keys. A Flink job with no idleness setting reads it and never emits a window. What is the likeliest cause?

choices.text: The bound is too small for the shops, so every sale is dropped as late
choices.why: A small bound emits early and drops more; it does not stop emission.

choices.text: Partitions with no key hold the minimum watermark at nothing
choices.why: Right. Five keys reach at most five of twelve partitions; the rest are empty.

choices.text: Twelve partitions are too many for Flink to track one watermark each
choices.why: Flink reads thousands; the trouble is that some are empty.

choices.text: The shops' clocks are wrong
choices.why: Wrong clocks give wrong windows, not none at all.

prompt: Put what happens to the 09:05 to 09:10 window (bound 2 minutes, lateness 5) in order.
items: Sales 4 and 5 are counted in it
Sale 6 moves the watermark past 09:10, and it is emitted with two sales
Sale 8 arrives late and updates it to three sales
Sale 10 moves the watermark past 09:15, and it is forgotten

prompt: Ponto Final wants sales per five minutes on a dashboard that upserts, plus exact daily totals for accounting. Which design fits the lesson?

choices.text: A bound of four hours, so that every number on the dashboard is exact and no batch is needed
choices.why: Every window would wait four hours; that is the batch, without its completeness.

choices.text: No watermark, and the dashboard reads the topic by arrival time
choices.why: That is lesson 9's wrong column.

choices.text: A short bound with lateness, late sales to a topic, and the nightly batch for the totals
choices.why: Right. Fast and nearly right on the dashboard, exact the next morning in the books.

choices.text: Emit each window once and drop late sales silently
choices.why: Silent drops make the accounting wrong with no trail.
